Think Dense, Not Long: Dynamic Decoupled Conditional Advantage
for Efficient Reasoning

Keqin Peng Affiliation: Beihang University Email: keqin.peng@buaa.edu.cn    Yuanxin Ouyang Affiliation: Beihang University Email: liangding.liam@gmail.com    Xuebo Liu Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen    Zhiliang Tian Affiliation: National University of Defense Technology    Ruijian Han Affiliation: Hong Kong Polytechnic University    Yancheng Yuan Affiliation: Hong Kong Polytechnic University    Liang Ding ††thanks: ˜˜Corresponding Authors. Affiliation: Alibaba Group
Abstract

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can elicit strong multi-step reasoning, yet it often encourages overly verbose traces. Moreover, naive length penalties in group-relative optimization can severely hurt accuracy. We attribute this failure to two structural issues: (i) Dilution of Length Baseline, where incorrect responses (with zero length reward) depress the group baseline and over-penalize correct solutions; and (ii) Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch, where a static penalty cannot adapt to problem difficulty, suppressing necessary reasoning on hard instances while leaving redundancy on easy ones. We propose Dynamic Decoupled Conditional Advantage (DDCA) to decouple efficiency optimization from correctness. DDCA computes length advantages conditionally within the correct-response cluster to eliminate baseline dilution, and dynamically scales the penalty strength using the group pass rate as a proxy for difficulty. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, and AIME25 show that DDCA consistently improves the efficiency–accuracy trade-off relative to adaptive baselines (e.g., Arora and Zanette, 2025), reducing generated tokens by approximately 60% on simpler tasks (e.g., GSM8K) versus over 20% on harder benchmarks (e.g., AIME25), thereby maintaining or improving accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/alphadl/DDCA.

1 Introduction

The advent of large reasoning models (LRMs), exemplified by OpenAI’s o111 1 https://openai.com/o1/ and DeepSeek-R1 Guo et al. (2025), has marked a paradigm shift in natural language processing from “System 1” rapid responses to “System 2” deliberate reasoning. By employing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting/verification (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), these models have achieved unprecedented success in complex mathematical and logical domains. However, this performance comes at a substantial cost: inference inefficiency. Models trained via standard RLVR, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), tend to develop a behavior we term “overthinking”—generating excessively verbose reasoning traces that inflate computational costs and latency without necessarily improving the final answer’s correctness.

Mitigating overthinking is critical for the scalable deployment of LRMs. A natural intuition is to incorporate a length penalty into the reward function to discourage verbosity. While straightforward, empirical evidence suggests that naively penalizing length often substantially degrades reasoning performance Su and Cardie (2025). The community faces a dilemma: we can have models that are accurate but verbose, or efficient but intellectually “shallow”.

In this work, we investigate the root cause of this trade-off. We argue that the failure of naive length penalties is not merely a hyperparameter tuning issue, but stems from structural issues in how correctness and efficiency signals interact under group-relative optimization. Through a theoretical decomposition of the GRPO objective, we identify two critical failures:

  • •

    The Dilution of Length Baseline: In standard group-relative estimation, the baseline is computed over all samples. Since incorrect responses typically receive zero reward (and thus carry no length signal), mixed-quality groups exhibit a systematically depressed baseline. As a result, even correct solutions can be over-penalized against an artificially low threshold. DDCA addresses this by computing length advantages only within the correct-response cluster.

  • •

    Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch: A static length penalty cannot adapt to problem difficulty. It tends to suppress necessary reasoning on hard problems (where longer traces are required for correctness), while being too weak to curb redundancy on easy problems. DDCA addresses this by scaling the efficiency pressure using the group pass rate, focusing on correctness for hard instances and efficiency for easy ones.

To resolve these issues, we propose Dynamic Decoupled Conditional Advantage (DDCA), a reward shaping framework compatible with GRPO and RLOO. DDCA disentangles efficiency from correctness with two coupled designs that map directly to the two failures above: (i) it computes length advantages conditionally within the correct-response cluster to eliminate baseline dilution; and (ii) it dynamically scales the penalty strength using the group pass rate to adapt length control to difficulty. We further apply a Sigmoid-based mapping to bound length signals, turning efficiency from a punitive constraint into a stable bonus for high information density.

We validate DDCA on the DeepSeek-R1-Distill (representing the SFT stage) and DeepScaleR (representing the further RL-refined stage) across four competitive benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, AIME25). Experimental results demonstrate that DDCA selectively optimizes costs based on difficulty: it reduces token consumption by approx. 60% on simpler tasks (e.g., GSM8K) while retaining 75–80% of the reasoning length on harder benchmarks (e.g., AIME25) to ensure correctness. Our work shows that we can teach models to think efficiently without forcing them to think less.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We dissect the failure of length-penalized RLVR, identifying the Dilution of Length Baseline and Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch as the structural causes of the efficiency–accuracy trade-off.

  • •

    We propose DDCA, a theoretically grounded framework that decouples correctness and efficiency via conditional (correct-only) length advantages and difficulty-aware scaling.

  • •

    Experiments show that DDCA achieves a strong efficiency–accuracy trade-off across model families and benchmarks.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), notably Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; Shao et al. (2024)), is an effective method for enhancing the reasoning ability of large language models. GRPO formulates a policy-gradient objective that removes the need for an explicit value function by using comparative advantage estimation within a group of sampled responses. Specifically, GRPO samples a group of responses {o1,o2,…,oG}\{o_{1},o_{2},\ldots,o_{\text{G}}\} for each question, assigns each response a verifiable reward r⁡(⋅)r(\cdot), and then estimates its advantage using the group mean and standard deviation of rewards:

A^i=r(oi)−mean({r(o1),r(o2),⋯,r(oG}))std({r(o1),r(o2),⋯,r(oG})).\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{r({o_{i}})-\text{mean}(\{r(o_{1}),r(o_{2}),\cdots,r({o_{\text{G}}}\}))}{\text{std}(\{r(o_{1}),r(o_{2}),\cdots,r(o_{\text{G}}\}))}. (1)

Similar to PPO Schulman et al. (2017), GRPO uses a clipped objective with KL penalty and optimizes the policy model πθ\pi_{\theta} by maximizing the following objective:

where

τi,t=πθ​(oi,t|q,oi,<t)πθold​(oi,t|q,oi,<t)\tau_{i,t}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})} (3)
𝔻KL(πθ∥πref)=1|oi|∑t=1|oi|logπθ​(oi,t|q,oi,<t)πref​(oi,t|q,oi,<t).\quad\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}})=\frac{1}{|o_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|o_{i}|}\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t})}. (4)

Here, |oi||o_{i}| is the sequence length of response oio_{i}. πref\pi_{\text{ref}} represents the reference model and the term 𝔻KL(πθ∥πref)\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) indicates a KL penalty term to limit how much the trained model πθ\pi_{\theta} can deviate from the reference model πref\pi_{\text{ref}}.

2.2 Rule-based Reward Modeling with Length Penalty

For mitigating the overthinking phenomenon, one of the most straightforward methods is to add a length-based reward along with the fundamental correctness reward RcR_{c} to encourage shorter yet correct responses (Su and Cardie, 2025; Arora and Zanette, 2025). Specifically, if adopting a monotonically decreasing length reward function R⁡(l)=−γ​lR(l)=-\gamma l that takes the sequence length ll as input, the combined reward is defined as:

R⁡(y^,y)={1−γ​|oi|,is_equivalent​(y^,y)0,otherwiseR(\hat{y},y)=\begin{cases}1-\gamma|o_{i}|,&\texttt{is\_equivalent}(\hat{y},y)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (5)

where yy is the ground-truth answer and y^\hat{y} is the predicted answer, and γ\gamma is a small factor to prevent the length reward from leading the overall reward, which could be adaptively computed (Su and Cardie, 2025) or preset as a hyperparameter (Team et al., 2025).

3 Revisiting Length Penalty in RLVR

While introducing a length penalty is a prevalent heuristic to mitigate the overthinking phenomenon in reasoning models, empirical observations indicate that naively mixing a length penalty with correctness rewards often leads to performance degradation. In this section, we analyze the standard coupled reward formulation and identify two critical issues: the Dilution of Length Baseline and Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch, which collectively hinder the model’s ability to balance reasoning depth and conciseness.

3.1 The Dilution of Length Baseline

Standard GRPO estimates the baseline using the mean reward of all samples in a group. Let a prompt qq generate a group of GG responses 𝒪={o1,…,oG}\mathcal{O}=\{o_{1},\dots,o_{G}\}. We denote the subset of correct responses as 𝒞⊂𝒪\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{O} with size nn, and incorrect responses as 𝒲\mathcal{W} with size G−nG-n. Using the reward function from Equation 5, the group mean μ\mu is calculated as:

μ\displaystyle\mu =1G​∑i=1GR⁡(y,oi)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}R(y,o_{i}) (6)
=1G​(∑oj∈𝒞(1−γ​|oj|)+∑ok∈𝒲0).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{G}\left(\sum_{o_{j}\in\mathcal{C}}(1-\gamma|o_{j}|)+\sum_{o_{k}\in\mathcal{W}}0\right).

Let L¯𝒞=1n​∑oj∈𝒞|oj|\bar{L}_{\mathcal{C}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{o_{j}\in\mathcal{C}}|o_{j}| be the average length of the correct responses. The group mean simplifies to:

μ=nG−γ​nG​L¯𝒞.\mu=\frac{n}{G}-\gamma\frac{n}{G}\bar{L}_{\mathcal{C}}. (7)

Now, consider the unnormalized advantage Air​a​w=R⁡(y,oi)−μA^{raw}_{i}=R(y,o_{i})-\mu for a specific correct response oi∈𝒞o_{i}\in\mathcal{C}. Substituting the terms:

Air​a​w\displaystyle A^{raw}_{i} =(1−γ​|oi|)−(nG−γ​nG​L¯𝒞)\displaystyle=(1-\gamma|o_{i}|)-\left(\frac{n}{G}-\gamma\frac{n}{G}\bar{L}_{\mathcal{C}}\right) (8)
=(1−nG)−γ⁡(|oi|−nG​L¯𝒞).\displaystyle=\left(1-\frac{n}{G}\right)-\gamma\left(|o_{i}|-\frac{n}{G}\bar{L}_{\mathcal{C}}\right).

Equation (8) reveals the Dilution of Length Baseline. Ideally, to evaluate the efficiency of oio_{i}, the term |oi||o_{i}| should be compared against the average length of valid solutions, L¯𝒞\bar{L}_{\mathcal{C}}. However, the standard formulation compares |oi||o_{i}| against a diluted baseline nG​L¯𝒞\frac{n}{G}\bar{L}_{\mathcal{C}}.

Since the pass rate nG≤1\frac{n}{G}\leq 1, the subtracted baseline is systematically smaller than the actual average length. This results in an exaggerated penalty term, where correct responses are punished not for being longer than peers, but for being longer than a baseline artificially lowered by incorrect (zero-reward) responses. This variance hinders the model from distinguishing between necessary reasoning and redundancy, particularly in early training stages where nn is small.

3.2 Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch

The second issue arises from applying a static penalty coefficient γ\gamma across problems of varying difficulty. We define the empirical difficulty of a problem inversely proportional to the group pass rate ρ=nG\rho=\frac{n}{G}.

High Difficulty (ρ→0\rho\to 0):

Hard problems typically require complex reasoning chains, implying a naturally higher token count (|oi||o_{i}| is large). However, as derived in Eq. (8), the penalty term is −γ​|oi|-\gamma|o_{i}|. If γ\gamma is static, this negative term can dominate the reward signal for long, correct chains. Consequently, the model is incentivized to shorten responses even when extensive reasoning is critical for accuracy, potentially collapsing the reasoning chain and degrading performance on hard tasks.

Low Difficulty (ρ→1\rho\to 1):

For easy problems, the model is confident, and the primary optimization objective should shift from correctness (which is already satisfied) to efficiency. A static γ\gamma chosen to accommodate hard problems is often too lenient for easy ones, failing to sufficiently penalize redundancy.

4 Methodology

To address the Dilution of Length Baseline and Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch identified in Section 3, we propose Dynamic Decoupled Conditional Advantage (DDCA). Our method decouples the optimization of reasoning correctness from token efficiency, employing a conditional RLOO estimator with dynamic difficulty scaling.

4.1 Decoupled Advantage Framework

Standard RLVR approaches typically mix correctness and length penalties into a single scalar reward. We propose decoupling the total advantage AiA_{i} into two independent components: the accuracy advantage AaccA^{\text{acc}} and the length penalty advantage AlenA^{\text{len}}. For a prompt xx and a group of NN sampled responses {y1,…,yN}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\}, the total advantage is formulated as:

Ai=Aiacc−β⋅AilenA_{i}=A_{i}^{\text{acc}}-\beta\cdot A_{i}^{\text{len}} (9)

where β\beta is a hyperparameter controlling the global penalty strength.

We employ the Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) estimator for both components to reduce gradient variance. The accuracy advantage is computed as:

Aiacc=riacc−1N−1​∑j≠irjaccA_{i}^{\text{acc}}=r_{i}^{\text{acc}}-\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j\neq i}r_{j}^{\text{acc}} (10)

where rjacc∈{0,1}r_{j}^{\text{acc}}\in\{0,1\} is the binary correctness label.

4.2 Dynamic Length Reward and Advantage

Another core innovation lies in the construction of the length advantage AilenA_{i}^{\text{len}}. This process involves three steps: (1) conditional length normalization, (2) Sigmoid reward modeling, and (3) dynamic RLOO estimation.

Conditional Sigmoid Reward.

To solve the baseline dilution problem, we first compute length statistics strictly within the subset of correct responses 𝒞={yj∣rjacc=1}\mathcal{C}=\{y_{j}\mid r_{j}^{\text{acc}}=1\}. For a correct response yi∈𝒞y_{i}\in\mathcal{C}, we calculate the Z-score of its length:

zi=|yi|−μ𝒞σ𝒞,where ​μ𝒞=1|𝒞|​∑yj∈𝒞|yj|.z_{i}=\frac{|y_{i}|-\mu_{\mathcal{C}}}{\sigma_{\mathcal{C}}},\quad\text{where }\mu_{\mathcal{C}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{y_{j}\in\mathcal{C}}|y_{j}|. (11)

Instead of using the raw Z-score, we define the length reward rilenr_{i}^{\text{len}} using a Sigmoid transformation:

rilen=Sigmoid​(zi)=11+e−zir_{i}^{\text{len}}=\text{Sigmoid}(z_{i})=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z_{i}}} (12)

This formulation yields a bounded reward rilen∈(0,1)r_{i}^{\text{len}}\in(0,1). Responses significantly longer than peers (zi≫0z_{i}\gg 0) receive a penalty reward close to 1, while concise responses approach 0. This normalization serves two purposes: it prevents extremely long "hallucinations" or short guesses (outliers) from dominating the gradient, and it ensures the penalty magnitude is comparable across different prompt lengths.

Dynamic RLOO Estimation.

Finally, we compute the length advantage AilenA_{i}^{\text{len}} using RLOO to minimize variance. Crucially, we incorporate the Difficulty-Aware Coefficient ρ=nN\rho=\frac{n}{N} (where n=|𝒞|n=|\mathcal{C}|) directly into this term.

For any correct response yi∈𝒞y_{i}\in\mathcal{C}, the dynamic length advantage is defined as:

Ailen=(nN)⏟Difficulty⋅(rilen−1n−1​∑j∈𝒞,j≠irjlen)⏟Conditional RLOOA_{i}^{\text{len}}=\underbrace{\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)}_{\text{Difficulty}}\cdot\underbrace{\left(r_{i}^{\text{len}}-\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C},j\neq i}r_{j}^{\text{len}}\right)}_{\text{Conditional RLOO}} (13)

For incorrect responses (yi∉𝒞y_{i}\notin\mathcal{C}), Ailen=0A_{i}^{\text{len}}=0.

Combining this with Eq. (9), our final DDCA objective adaptively modulates the optimization focus:

  • •

    Hard Problems (n/N→0n/N\to 0): The coefficient nN\frac{n}{N} suppresses the length advantage. The model focuses purely on AaccA^{\text{acc}}, prioritizing the discovery of correct reasoning paths regardless of length.

  • •

    Easy Problems (n/N→1n/N\to 1): The coefficient approaches 1. The model is penalized for having a higher rlenr^{\text{len}} than its peers, driving it towards the most efficient solution within the correct cluster.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Training.

We choose two representative reasoning models: DeepScaleR - 1.5B - Preview and DeepSeek - R1 - Distill - Qwen - 1.5B (Guo et al., 2025) as our backbone models, which have shown strong performance on mathematical reasoning tasks. Following Hou et al. (2025), we view them as two representative post-training paradigms. Specifically, DeepSeek-R1-Distill is obtained by supervised fine-tuning on DeepSeek-R1 outputs, which may limit its ceiling. In contrast, DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview further applies RL on top of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B.

For the training dataset, since prior work Ye et al. (2025) has shown that even a small but high-quality dataset can improve LLM performance via RL, we use a compact training set consisting only of historical AIME and AMC math questions. Following Hou et al. (2025), we use the preprocessed data from Prime Cui et al. (2025) and take the AIME–AMC subset for training. In total, the training dataset consists of 2470 distinct training examples.

Evaluation.

We evaluate the models on four test datasets: GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), which contains grade-school-level math problems; MATH500 Lightman et al. (2023), a standard benchmark with harder problems than GSM8K; AMC23; and the American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) 2025, two competition-level datasets of challenging mathematical problems. For fair comparison, we set the temperature to 0.6, top-pp to 0.95, and use a maximum token limit of 16384 suggested by (Guo et al., 2025). We conduct 4 rollouts for GSM8K and MATH500 due to their large number of test samples, and 16 rollouts for AMC23 and AIME 2025 to compute pass@1. We also compute the Average Efficiency Score Luo et al. (2025) for a comprehensive assessment of efficiency and efficacy.

5.2 Metrics

We use AES and pass@1 to evaluate our method.

AES.

Let p=pass​@​1p=\mathrm{pass@1}, pb=pass​@​1basep_{b}=\mathrm{pass@1}_{\mathrm{base}}, LL be the average token cost, and LbL_{b} be the base policy token cost. The AES score (Luo et al., 2025) is defined as:

AES=\displaystyle\mathrm{AES}\;= Lb−LLb+{3​p−pbpb,p≥pb,−5​pb−ppb,p<pb.\displaystyle\frac{L_{b}-L}{L_{b}}+\begin{cases}3\,\dfrac{p-p_{b}}{p_{b}},&p\geq p_{b},\\[2.0pt] -5\,\dfrac{p_{b}-p}{p_{b}},&p<p_{b}.\end{cases} (14)

This metric rewards token reduction while heavily penalizing performance drops and favoring improvements over the baseline.

Pass@K.

The pass@K (Chen, 2021) scores are computed as below:

pass​@​K=1−(n−cK)(nK)\mathrm{pass@K}=1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{K}}{\binom{n}{K}} (15)

where nn is the number of samples and cc is the number of correct samples. When KK is set to 1, this metric is reduced to the average accuracy among the nn samples.

Baselines.

We compare our proposed DDCA against:

  • •

    Vanilla RLOO: The standard algorithm without explicit length constraints.

  • •

    GRPO+LP: A Standard GRPO with a linear length penalty.

  • •

    ThinkPrune-4K Hou et al. (2025): A length-clip reward to compress CoT length. We set the maximum length equal 4K.

  • •

    TLMRE Su and Cardie (2025): An efficient training method with non-linear length penalty.

6 Main Results

We evaluate DDCA on four reasoning benchmarks spanning elementary to competition-level difficulty (GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, AIME25) and two backbone models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview). Table 1 summarizes the accuracy–efficiency trade-off against representative baselines.

DDCA improves the efficiency–accuracy trade-off. As shown in Table 1, Ours (DDCA) consistently achieves the highest Accuracy-Efficiency Score (AES) across both model backbones (0.42 for DeepSeek-R1 and 0.30 for DeepScaleR). Compared to the strong +RLOO baseline on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, DDCA not only improves average accuracy by 0.4% (68.1%→68.5%68.1\%\rightarrow 68.5\%) but also substantially reduces average token consumption by approximately 20% (6061→49086061\rightarrow 4908). Even on the already optimized DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview, DDCA reduces token usage by over 1,000 tokens on average (4182→30954182\rightarrow 3095) while maintaining comparable accuracy (72.2%72.2\% vs. 72.5%72.5\%). This confirms that decoupling the length advantage and applying conditional normalization allows the model to cut redundancy without sacrificing reasoning capabilities.

DDCA preserves reasoning capacity on hard tasks.

The benefits of our dynamic difficulty-aware mechanism are most pronounced on challenging benchmarks. Standard length penalties (+LP) often degrade performance on hard tasks (e.g., dropping AIME25 accuracy from 25.0% to 23.3% on DeepSeek-R1) by prematurely truncating necessary reasoning chains. In contrast, DDCA achieves the highest accuracy of 26.5% on AIME25 with the DeepSeek backbone, outperforming both TLMRE (25.0%) and ThinkPrune-4k (25.2%). This validates that scaling the penalty by the pass rate (nN\frac{n}{N}) effectively relaxes constraints for difficult problems, preserving the "deep thinking" capacity required for competition-level mathematics while aggressively optimizing efficiency on easier tasks like GSM8K (where tokens are reduced to ∼\sim1200).

7 Analysis

We further conduct a comprehensive analysis to investigate the properties of DDCA from three perspectives: capability, mechanism, and sensitivity. First, we evaluate the method’s capabilities by examining its scalability across varying token budgets (Section 7.1) and its ability to maintain exploration diversity (Section 7.2). Next, we validate the underlying mechanisms, quantifying the specific mitigation of baseline dilution (Section 7.3) and verifying the contribution of each design component through ablation studies (Section 7.4). Finally, we analyze the hyperparameter sensitivity regarding the penalty coefficient β\beta to provide practical usage insights (Section 7.5).

7.1 Scalability across Token Budgets

We evaluate DDCA across varying token budgets (2k to 16k). Figure 1 presents the results on AMC23 and AIME25.

As shown in Figure 1, DDCA consistently improves accuracy while curbing token usage. On the challenging AIME25 dataset (right column), the dynamic difficulty coefficient (nN\frac{n}{N}) allows the model to utilize deeper reasoning when needed, resulting in a +4.6%+4.6\% accuracy gain at 16k budget, while still reducing the average computational cost by maintaining conciseness on solved sub-paths.

7.2 Exploration Capability Analysis

We further investigate whether the length penalty in DDCA hinders the model’s exploration capability. Figure 2 presents the Pass@K performance (K∈{1,…,16}K\in\{1,\dots,16\}).

As shown in Figure 2, DDCA (solid lines) maintains a consistent performance margin over the Baseline (dashed lines). Crucially, on the hard AIME25 benchmark, the slope of our Pass@K curve remains steep. This indicates that DDCA does not suffer from mode collapse; instead, the dynamic coefficient nN\frac{n}{N} successfully acts as a regularizer, encouraging the model to explore diverse yet concise reasoning trajectories.

7.3 Mitigation of Baseline Dilution

To empirically verify that DDCA mitigates the Dilution of Length Baseline, we analyzed the performance on the MATH-500 benchmark, stratified by problem difficulty (Levels 1-5). Baseline dilution occurs when incorrect responses (with effectively zero length penalty contribution) pull down the group mean, distorting the advantage estimation. This phenomenon is theoretically most severe in hard problems where the pass rate is low (i.e., mixed-quality groups are common).

The results in Figure 3 confirm our hypothesis:

  • •

    Level 1-2 (Easy): The pass rates are high (∼94%\sim 94\%), meaning groups consist almost entirely of correct responses. Here, baseline dilution is negligible, and DDCA performs comparably to TLMRE (94.2%94.2\% vs. 94.0%94.0\%).

  • •

    Level 5 (Hard): The pass rates drop to ∼70%\sim 70\%, introducing significant variance in response quality within groups. Standard methods like TLMRE suffer here because the length baseline is diluted by incorrect answers. In contrast, DDCA decouples the efficiency estimation, comparing correct solutions only against other correct ones. Consequently, we observe the largest performance gain of +1.2% (70.6%→71.8%70.6\%\to 71.8\%) in this high-difficulty regime.

This demonstrates that our decoupled advantage formulation effectively robustifies the reward signal against the noise introduced by incorrect samples, a critical property for solving complex reasoning tasks.

7.4 Component Ablation Study

To verify the distinct contributions of the Decoupled Advantage and the Dynamic Difficulty Coefficient (nN\frac{n}{N}), we examine the performance of DDCA variants on both MATH (easy) and AIME25 (hard) datasets. The results are summarized in Table 2.

Impact of Dynamic Coefficient (w/o Dynamic).

The "w/o Dynamic" variant applies a static decoupled penalty. While it achieves the lowest token usage on MATH-500 dataset, it suffers significantly on the hard AIME25 task, yielding a low accuracy of 21.9%. This confirms the Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch: a static penalty indiscriminately truncates the extensive reasoning chains required for complex problems. In contrast, the full DDCA utilizes the dynamic term to relax the penalty for hard tasks, restoring accuracy to 26.5%.

Impact of Decoupling (w/o Decouple).

The "w/o Decouple" variant incorporates the difficulty coefficient but calculates advantage across the mixed group (including incorrect responses). On the easy MATH dataset, it fails to significantly reduce token consumption compared to the baseline (4662→39734662\to 3973). This validates the existence of Baseline Dilution: the inclusion of incorrect responses lowers the reward baseline, weakening the efficiency signal. DDCA resolves this by decoupling the baseline, successfully compressing the reasoning path.

Conclusion.

DDCA effectively synergizes both components. The Decoupling mechanism ensures precise efficiency optimization for solvable problems, while the Dynamic mechanism acts as a safety guard to preserve reasoning depth for difficult problems.

7.5 Sensitivity Analysis of Penalty Coefficient

We investigate the trade-off between reasoning accuracy and token efficiency by varying the penalty coefficient β∈{0.2,0.3,0.5}\beta\in\{0.2,0.3,0.5\}. Figure 4 illustrates the results on MATH500 and AIME25.

Trade-off Analysis.

The results demonstrate a clear dichotomy. On the easier MATH500 benchmark, increasing β\beta from 0.2 to 0.3 improves accuracy by removing redundant reasoning steps ("overthinking"). However, on the harder AIME25 benchmark, any increase in β\beta strictly degrades accuracy, as the penalty truncates the extensive exploration required for complex solutions. In all cases, token usage (Orange) decreases monotonically with β\beta. This justifies our dynamic mechanism: applying stricter penalties on easy tasks while relaxing them on hard ones.

8 Related Work

Reinforcement Learning For Reasoning.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used for post-training large language models, especially to improve multi-step reasoning. Alignment-oriented post-training methods such as RLHF have become standard recipes (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Garg et al., 2025), and reasoning-oriented post-training has been revitalized by long-thinking LRMs such as OpenAI’s o122 2 https://openai.com/o1/ and DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025). Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) further enables learning from automatically checkable outcomes (e.g., math and code) (Liu and Zhang, 2025), with algorithmic advances such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and DAPO (Yu et al., 2025). Complementary analyses also show that deeper problem understanding can boost math reasoning performance (Zhong et al., 2024), and explicit reasoning chains can improve robustness in related settings (Wu et al., 2025). Beyond RL-based post-training, in-context learning performance is also sensitive to demonstration selection strategies (Peng et al., 2024). Our work targets a distinct issue: efficiency constraints can distort group-relative RLVR advantages; we address this via advantage-level reward shaping to preserve correctness while controlling length.

Length Penalty for Efficient Reasoning.

Overly long reasoning traces (overthinking) increase inference costs (Chen et al., 2024) and may be driven by repeated re-verification (self-doubt) (Peng et al., 2025). A range of approaches have been explored (Zhu and Li, 2025), with a common direction integrating length awareness into RL. For example, Arora and Zanette (2025) ranks sampled solutions by correctness and normalized length, while Song et al. Song and Zheng (2025) improve GRPO (GRPO++/L-GRPO) with additional mechanisms for stable training. Unlike these coupled or static formulations, DDCA decouples efficiency from correctness at the advantage level by computing length advantages only among correct responses and scaling efficiency pressure by pass rate, directly addressing baseline dilution and difficulty mismatch.

9 Conclusion

In this work, we revisit the length penalty in RLVR and identify the Dilution of Length Baseline and Difficulty-Penalty Mismatch as two fundamental flaws in standard group-relative optimization. We show that coupled rewards inevitably lead to either uncontrollable length collapse in easy tasks or the suppression of reasoning in hard tasks. We propose Dynamic Decoupled Conditional Advantage (DDCA), which decouples the efficiency objective and applies it conditionally to correct responses. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DDCA achieves a superior Pareto frontier, reducing token consumption by up to 60% on easier benchmarks while preserving the "deep thinking" capacity required for hard tasks (e.g., AIME25). Our findings highlight that efficient reasoning requires incentivizing higher information density within valid reasoning paths, rather than simply penalizing length. We hope DDCA serves as a robust baseline for future research in efficient System 2 scaling.

Limitations

While our proposed DDCA demonstrates significant improvements in reasoning efficiency, we acknowledge several limitations:

  • •

    Domain Specificity: Our theoretical analysis and experiments focus primarily on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks (STEM), where "correctness" is binary and verifiable. The applicability of DDCA to open-ended generation or creative writing tasks, where the definition of "efficiency" is more subjective, remains to be explored.

  • •

    Hyperparameter Sensitivity: Although DDCA is more robust than vanilla length penalties, the efficiency coefficient β\beta still requires tuning. An overly aggressive β\beta might still encourage the model to skip necessary verification steps in extremely hard problems, albeit to a lesser extent than baseline methods.

Appendix A Implementation Details

We build on the Verl codebase Sheng et al. (2025)33 3 We also implement our method upon slime Zhu et al. (2025) in our code.. For all experiments, we utilize four RTX-5090 GPUs on a single low-density node. We set vLLM to maximum context length (16K) during generation and set the generation temperature to 0.6. For training, we set the maximum response equal 8192 and generate 8 responses for each prompt. For every iteration, 8 prompts are selected from the dataset and the global batch size is set to 32. For the 1.5B, the learning rate is set to 2e-6, and the value of the KL coefficient is set to 1e-3. We use the same prompt template for all models, which can be found below:

$QUESTION. Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.
